title: Active control of THz plasmon propagation in a one-dimensional electronic waveguide
authors: Thomas Vasselon, Uzer Ahmad, Clément Geffroy, Lucas Mazzella, Matteo Aluffi, Seddik Ouacel, Jashwanth Shaju, Kevin Bredillet, Nathan Roussel, Jean-François Roux, Pierre-Baptiste Vigneron, Arne Ludwig, Andreas D. Wieck, Matias Urdampilleta, Hermann Sellier, Giorgos Georgiou, Christopher Bäuerle
abstract: Quantum nanoelectronics is pushing towards ever higher operating frequencies in order to realise quantum technologies capable of processing information at unprecedented speeds. A particularly promising direction is the development of flying electron qubits, which offer the prospect of quantum operations on picosecond timescales. Achieving in-flight quantum control in this regime would establish a fundamentally new paradigm for studying quantum entanglement and enable a novel form of quantum information processing based on propagating electronic wavepackets. Here we report a first step towards this goal by injecting ultrashort electron wavepackets into an engineered quantum nanoelectronic device. We demonstrate active control over the propagation speed of an electron wavepacket with a temporal duration as short as 4 ps in a quasi-one-dimensional electron waveguide with a length ranging from 10 $\mathrmμ$m to 40 $\mathrmμ$m. This advance provides a key building block for ultrafast quantum operations using flying electrons. Beyond its technological implications, our approach offers a platform for exploring the intrinsic dynamical processes that govern quantum transport and coherence in nanoscale electronic systems.
summary: The researchers report an experiment demonstrating active control over THz plasmon propagation in a gated 1D electronic waveguide. By measuring the time-domain response of the plasmons while tuning the gate voltage, they successfully extracted the plasmon velocity, confirming a theoretical square-root dependence on the waveguide's conductance. This work establishes a key building block for ultrafast quantum operations using propagating electron wavepackets.
main_problem: The primary goal is to achieve and demonstrate active control over the propagation speed of ultrashort electron wavepackets (THz plasmons) within a quasi-one-dimensional electronic waveguide.
main_result: The experiment successfully demonstrated that the plasmon propagation velocity ($v_{1D}$) can be actively tuned by varying the electrostatic gate voltage, showing a clear square-root dependence on the waveguide conductance ($v_{1D} \propto \sqrt{G}$).
method: Time-resolved THz spectroscopy was employed, using photoconductive switches to generate femtosecond/picosecond pulses that excite plasmons in a gated 2DEG waveguide. Velocity was extracted by analyzing the time delay ($	au$) or the separation ($\delta$) of interference fringes as a function of gate voltage.
model_or_system: The physical system is a quantum nanoelectronic device built on a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure, featuring a quasi-1D electron waveguide (2DEG) integrated with coplanar waveguides (CPWs) for THz excitation/detection. The system is controlled electrostatically via gate voltages.
key_observables: Transmitted THz current amplitude, time delay ($	au$) of interference fringes, and fringe separation ($\delta$) as functions of gate voltage.
important_parameters: Picosecond timescales (e.g., 4 ps pulse duration), THz frequencies, and the dependence of velocity on conductance ($G$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the plasmonic excitation remains effectively one-dimensional, and the measured signal is dominated by the plasmonic propagation through the gated 2DEG, filtering out background substrate/capacitive coupling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device schematic, the dependence of the transmitted THz pulse on gate voltage, and plots showing the extracted plasmon velocity ($v_{1D}$) dependence on conductance, confirming the $\sqrt{G}$ scaling.
paper_structure: The paper details the device architecture, describes the time-resolved measurement techniques using PCSs, and then presents multiple analyses (using both $	au$ and $\delta$ methods) to extract the plasmon velocity, consistently confirming the $\sqrt{G}$ scaling law.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controlled, solid-state platform for studying fundamental quantum transport phenomena (plasmon dynamics) at THz frequencies, which is relevant for understanding energy dissipation and coherent electron dynamics in nanoscale quantum devices.
